1.notes: Andreae was an ordained Lutheran pastor throughout his career; the Rosicrucian manifestos reflected a utopian-reformist Lutheran program rather than Hermetic initiation

2.notes: Dee was conformist Church of England; his Hermetic and angelic philosophy was a scholarly program layered over Protestant practice

3.notes: Fludd was a practising English physician and Church of England conformist whose Hermetic cosmology was his philosophical not confessional identity

4.notes: Paracelsus was buried as a Catholic in Salzburg; his theological allegiances were complex and independent of Lutheran or Reformed confessions, but his sacramental realism and Marian references lean Catholic

5.notes: Böhme was baptised and buried Lutheran; his visionary theosophy was developed within a Lutheran spiritual framework though it frequently transgressed Lutheran orthodoxy

6.notes: Ashmole was a Royalist Anglican who engaged with alchemy as an antiquarian-scholarly pursuit alongside his Royalist religious commitments

7.notes: Swedenborg was raised and remained nominally Lutheran; his visionary theology eventually developed into the New Jerusalem Church, which remained distinct from mainstream Lutheranism

8.notes: Eckartshausen was a Bavarian Catholic court councillor who never left the Roman Church; his mysticism was developed within a Catholic framework and was explicitly hostile to Protestant rationalism

9.notes: Saint-Martin was raised Catholic; his theosophy drew heavily on Böhme but he maintained Catholic affinities throughout his life, though his mysticism transcended confessional boundaries

10.notes: Maier was a Lutheran physician who became one of the most earnest public defenders of the Rosicrucian brotherhood; his alchemical work was conducted within a Protestant-Hermetic synthesis

11.notes: Thomas Vaughan (born 1622) was an Anglican clergyman ejected for Royalism; his Hermetic-alchemical writing was the work of a practising if unconventional Anglican

12.notes: Francis Bacon was a conformist Church of England figure; his natural philosophy was deliberately separated from theological commitments though he remained formally Anglican

13.notes: Bruno was a former Dominican friar; he left the order but never formally renounced Catholicism, and his Hermetism was in tension with both Catholic orthodoxy and Protestant reformism — ultimately executed by the Roman Inquisition

14.notes: Khunrath's Amphitheatrum Sapientiae Aeternae explicitly integrates Lutheran piety with Hermetic-alchemical philosophy; he was a Lutheran physician in Hamburg and Dresden

15.notes: Catherine of Siena was a Dominican tertiary and Doctor of the Catholic Church; entirely within Roman Catholic devotional tradition

16.notes: Ficino was ordained as a Catholic priest in 1473 and remained a canon of Florence cathedral; his Platonism was pursued within a Catholic humanist framework

17.notes: Pico della Mirandola was a Catholic layman and eventually a devotee of Savonarola; his Christian Kabbalah and Hermetism were pursued as extensions of Catholic theology

18.notes: Nicolas Flamel (born c.1330) was a Parisian Catholic bourgeois; the alchemical legend attached to him developed within a Catholic devotional and charitable framework

19.notes: Jabir ibn Hayyan was a Muslim (Ismaili Shia affiliation in some sources); not Jewish — classification revised: primary affiliation is Ismaili Shia Islam, but Jewish is not applicable

20.notes: Hermes Trismegistus is a legendary-syncretic figure; the Hermetic Corpus synthesizes late antique Egyptian, Greek, and Jewish religious ideas without belonging to any single confession

21.notes: Thomas Aquinas was a Dominican friar and Doctor of the Church; the foundational scholastic theologian of Roman Catholicism

22.notes: Roger Bacon was a Franciscan friar; his natural philosophy was pursued within a Catholic mendicant framework

23.notes: Plotinus preceded Christianity and his philosophy is the source tradition for Neoplatonism; affiliation is philosophical rather than confessional

24.notes: Blake was baptised Anglican but developed a syncretic spiritual vision profoundly influenced by Böhme, Swedenborg (critically), and his own mythological system; his primary philosophical affiliation is visionary-theosophical

25.notes: Louis-Claude de Saint-Martin (the 'Unknown Philosopher') was raised and died Catholic; his Böhmist theosophy was developed within rather than against his Catholicism

26.notes: Gichtel was raised Lutheran but his mystical Behmenism led to separation from institutional church life; he founded the celibate 'Angel Brethren' community in Amsterdam as an extra-ecclesiastical Böhmist group

27.notes: Weishaupt was a Bavarian Catholic who founded the Illuminati as an Enlightenment rationalist project within a Catholic social milieu; his relationship to Catholicism was increasingly hostile but he was formed within it

28.notes: Cagliostro was a Sicilian Catholic who engaged with Freemasonry, Egyptian Rite, and popular magic within a broadly Catholic cultural context

29.notes: Gerhard Dorn was a Paracelsian physician who operated in Lutheran territories; his alchemical-theosophical writing drew on Paracelsian medicine within a Protestant intellectual framework

30.notes: Leonhard Thurneiser zum Thurn was a Paracelsian physician and polymath who worked in Berlin under the Protestant Hohenzollern court

31.notes: Catherine de Medici was a Florentine Catholic and Queen of France; her interest in astrology and alchemy was characteristic of Renaissance Catholic court culture

32.notes: Giambattista della Porta was a Neapolitan Catholic natural philosopher; his natural magic was pursued within a Catholic humanist framework, and he founded the Accademia dei Segreti

33.notes: Agrippa (born 1486) was raised and remained nominally Catholic throughout a peripatetic career, though his Three Books engaged with magic, Kabbalah, and Hermetism in ways that attracted ecclesiastical criticism; he died before the confessional hardening of the Reformation

34.notes: Rudolf II was Holy Roman Emperor and formally Catholic, though his court at Prague was ecumenically tolerant and attracted Protestant, Jewish, and Rosicrucian scholars; his personal religiosity leaned toward Hermetic-philosophical syncretism

35.notes: Trithemius was abbot of Sponheim and Würzburg — a Benedictine monk and Catholic churchman; his cryptography, natural magic, and angelic invocations were pursued within a Catholic monastic framework

36.notes: Samuel Fictuld was an eighteenth-century German Rosicrucian whose writings promoted the Gold- und Rosenkreutz order within a Lutheran cultural context

37.notes: Leibniz was a German Lutheran who engaged with Rosicrucian ideas early in his career; his mature philosophy synthesized Christian metaphysics with Neoplatonic rationalism within a broadly Lutheran Protestant context

38.notes: Joseph Glanvill was an Anglican clergyman and Fellow of the Royal Society; his defence of the reality of witchcraft and spirits was conducted within a moderate Anglican framework influenced by Cambridge Platonism

39.notes: Henry Khunrath (duplicate entry with id 14) was a Lutheran physician; same affiliation as id 14

40.notes: Philip Sidney was a Protestant courtier and poet in Elizabethan England; his engagement with Hermetic and Platonic ideas was characteristic of Protestant humanist culture

41.notes: Mary Anne Atwood (1817-1910) was a Victorian English woman whose spiritual alchemy drew on Böhmist-theosophical tradition within a broadly Anglican Protestant milieu

42.notes: Anna Zieglerin operated in Lutheran court contexts in Germany; her alchemical-prophetic claims drew on a Lutheran millenarian framework combined with Paracelsian medicine

43.notes: Johann Siebmacher was a Nuremberg heraldist and engraver who worked in Lutheran Germany; his connection to the Rosicrucian emblem tradition situates him in the Lutheran-Hermetic milieu

44.notes: George Cheyne was a Scottish-born physician who converted to a broadly Anglican pietism influenced by Böhmist and mystical traditions; his dietary spirituality connected physical and spiritual regeneration

45.notes: Johann Arndt was a Lutheran pastor and theologian whose True Christianity was a foundational text of Lutheran Pietism; his mystical theology drew on medieval German mysticism and Paracelsian nature philosophy

46.notes: Jane Lead was raised Anglican and developed her Böhmist prophetic mysticism within an English Protestant context; she founded the Philadelphian Society as a cross-denominational mystical fellowship

47.notes: Isaac Newton was a practising if heterodox Anglican; his alchemical work was conducted alongside his Arian theology and biblical chronology — all three were aspects of a unified search for hidden divine principles in nature and scripture

48.notes: Henry More was a Cambridge Platonist and Anglican clergyman who engaged critically with Böhme, Descartes, and the Hermetic tradition; his Neoplatonism was developed within an Anglican theological framework

49.notes: Benedict Chabotas (fl. c.1580) was a German Paracelsian physician associated with Lutheran court culture in the Holy Roman Empire

50.notes: Adam McLean (b.1947) is a contemporary Scottish scholar and practitioner of alchemy who has worked within broadly Protestant cultural context; his affiliation is primarily scholarly-Hermetic rather than confessional

51.notes: Brian Vickers (b.1937) is a contemporary English literary scholar; his affiliation is secular-academic rather than confessional

52.notes: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (duplicate of id 33) — Catholic with Hermetic secondary affiliation

53.notes: Thomas Vaughan (duplicate entry with id 11) was an ejected Anglican clergyman and Hermetic-alchemical author

54.notes: Zosimos of Panopolis (fl. c.300 CE) was an Alexandrian alchemist who operated in a syncretic late antique milieu drawing on Egyptian, Greek, Jewish Gnostic, and early Christian elements; Hermetist is the most applicable label

55.notes: Arnauld de Villeneuve (born c.1240) was a Catalan-French physician who served popes and kings; his alchemical writings circulated within a Catholic learned milieu

56.notes: Jean d'Espagnet (born 1564) was a French Catholic magistrate and Hermetic philosopher; his Enchiridion Physicae Restitutae and Arcanum Hermeticae Philosophiae are sophisticated Hermetic texts composed within French Catholic culture

57.notes: Anna Kingsford was raised Anglican but moved through Catholicism (received into the Roman Church) toward a theosophical-vegetarian mysticism; her primary intellectual affiliation is the nineteenth-century theosophical current

58.notes: Éliphas Lévi (Alphonse Louis Constant) was ordained as a Catholic deacon before abandoning his orders; his occult philosophy drew on Catholic ritual, Kabbalah, and Hermetism in equal measure, and he sought reconciliation with Rome in his final years

59.notes: William Law was a Non-Juror Anglican divine who became the leading English translator and interpreter of Jacob Böhme; his Behmenism was developed within an Anglican mystical framework

60.notes: Joseph Ennemoser was a Tyrolean Catholic physician and historian of magic; his History of Magic was written within a Catholic Bavarian cultural context with Romantic-idealist overtones

61.notes: Johann Georg Gichtel (duplicate entry with id 26) — Lutheran with Böhmist secondary affiliation

62.notes: Arthur Edward Waite (1857-1942) was born Catholic but spent most of his life within Anglican and Hermetic contexts; his primary affiliation is the Victorian-Edwardian Hermetic revival centered on the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn

63.notes: Iuliana Covaci (fl. c.1640) was a Romanian alchemist operating in a predominantly Eastern Orthodox or Catholic cultural context depending on the region; Catholic is the best approximation for a Romanian figure of this period in Transylvania

64.notes: Paracelsus (duplicate entry with id 4) — Catholic burial with Paracelsian philosophical affiliation

65.notes: Jacques Gohory (born c.1520) was a French Catholic humanist who was one of the first French translators and promoters of Paracelsus; his Paracelsianism was pursued within a French Catholic learned culture

66.notes: Symphorien Champier (born 1471) was a Lyonnais Catholic physician and humanist; his work synthesized Ficinian Neoplatonism with Galenism within a French Catholic humanist framework

67.notes: Jean Thibault (born c.1530) was a French Catholic physician and astrologer who promoted Paracelsian medicine at the French court

68.notes: Adam von Bodenstein (born 1528) was a Basel physician and one of the most important early editors of Paracelsus's works; he operated in the Reformed/Lutheran milieu of Basel

69.notes: Johannes Guinter of Andernach (born 1505) was a German physician who trained Vesalius and later in life translated Greek medical texts; he remained Catholic despite the Reformation pressures of his Strasbourg milieu

70.notes: Leonhard Fuchs (born 1501) was a German botanist and physician who became a committed Lutheran during the Reformation; his botanical work was pursued within a Protestant academic framework

71.notes: Jan Baptist van Helmont was a Flemish Catholic who faced Inquisition proceedings for his natural philosophy; he remained devoutly Catholic throughout his life, and his mystical chemistry was framed within a Catholic theological context

72.notes: Joseph Duchesne / Quercetanus (born c.1522) was a French Huguenot physician who served the French crown as a Paracelsian; his Calvinism coexisted with his Paracelsian medicine

73.notes: Oswald Croll (born c.1563) was a German Paracelsian physician who worked in Lutheran and Reformed Protestant territories; his Basilica Chymica is a major systematization of Paracelsian iatrochemistry

74.notes: William Bradwardine (born c.1495) appears to be a different figure from the medieval theologian Thomas Bradwardine; if this is a sixteenth-century figure, Catholic is most plausible for an English physician of that birth date

75.notes: Balthasar Walther (born c.1558) was a German physician and Paracelsian who studied Kabbalah in the Ottoman lands and returned to become part of the Rosicrucian circle around Andreae in Görlitz; his Lutheran background combined with esoteric Kabbalistic interests

76.notes: Michael Sendivogius (born c.1566) was a Polish Catholic alchemist and courtier who served both Catholic and Protestant princes; his alchemical philosophy was Catholic in formation and practice

77.notes: Louis Camelle (born c.1540) was a French Catholic physician associated with Paracelsian medicine at the French court

78.notes: Pierre Potier (born c.1535) was a French Catholic physician and promoter of Paracelsian chemical medicine; his practice was within the French Catholic learned culture

79.notes: Godefridus Steidel (born c.1540) was a Flemish Catholic physician associated with the Paracelsian tradition in the Spanish Netherlands

80.notes: Alonso Pena (born c.1505) was a Spanish Catholic physician; Spanish alchemists of this period operated within a thoroughly Catholic cultural framework

81.notes: Antoine de Gohorry (born c.1545) was a French Catholic humanist and early promoter of Paracelsian ideas in France

82.notes: Henri Rantzau (born 1526) was a Danish-German Lutheran nobleman and patron of scholars; his interest in astrology and occult philosophy was pursued within a Protestant aristocratic context

83.notes: Andreas Libavius (born c.1540) was a German Lutheran physician and chemist whose Alchemia systematized chemical practice; his Lutheranism was conservative and he was explicitly critical of Paracelsian mysticism even while systematizing chemical knowledge

84.notes: Tycho Brahe (born 1546) was a Danish Lutheran astronomer who also practiced alchemy; his Lutheranism coexisted with alchemical and astrological interests typical of the Hermetic natural philosophy tradition

85.notes: John Dee (duplicate entry with id 2) — Anglican with Hermetic secondary affiliation

86.notes: Giambattista della Porta (duplicate entry with id 32) — Catholic with Neoplatonist secondary affiliation

87.notes: Franciscus Sylvius (Frans de le Boe, born 1614) was a Flemish-Dutch physician and chemist at Leiden; the Dutch Republic milieu was predominantly Reformed/Calvinist, and Sylvius worked within this Protestant academic culture

88.notes: Robert Boyle (born 1627) was an Anglo-Irish Protestant with broadly Calvinist sympathies who engaged deeply with alchemy; his 'corpuscular philosophy' emerged from a chymical laboratory practice that he combined with devout Protestant piety

89.notes: Bernard Palissy (born c.1510) was a French Huguenot potter and naturalist who suffered imprisonment for his Reformed faith; his naturalistic philosophy combined Protestant empiricism with Hermetic sympathies

90.notes: Michael Maier (duplicate entry with id 10) — Lutheran with Rosicrucian secondary affiliation

91.notes: Johann Arndt (duplicate entry with id 45) — Lutheran Pietist with Böhmist/mystical secondary affiliation

92.notes: Gerhard Dorn (duplicate entry with id 29) — Lutheran Paracelsian physician

93.notes: Jabir ibn Hayyan (Geber, duplicate entry with id 19) was a Muslim practitioner; Hermetist is the closest available label for his syncretic alchemical-philosophical tradition

94.notes: al-Razi (born 854) was a Persian Muslim physician and alchemist; his natural philosophy drew on Greek Neoplatonic sources alongside Islamic medicine; Hermetist best captures his syncretic alchemical tradition in this taxonomy

95.notes: Albertus Magnus (born c.1193) was a Dominican friar, bishop, and Doctor of the Church; his engagement with alchemy and natural philosophy was conducted within a Catholic scholastic framework

96.notes: Roger Bacon (duplicate entry with id 22) was a Franciscan friar and Catholic natural philosopher

97.notes: Nicolas Flamel (duplicate entry with id 18) was a French Catholic bourgeois; the alchemical legend developed within a Catholic devotional context

98.notes: Arnaldus de Villanova (born c.1240) was a Catalan Catholic physician who served kings and popes; his alchemical writings circulated widely in the later medieval Catholic learned world

99.notes: Meister Eckhart (born c.1260) was a Dominican friar and theologian whose speculative mysticism was condemned by papal bull (In agro dominico, 1329); he remained within the Dominican order throughout his life

100.notes: Johann Tauler (born c.1300) was a Dominican friar and mystic in the tradition of Eckhart; his sermons were enormously influential on Lutheran Pietism (Luther edited them) but Tauler himself was a Catholic Dominican
